expectations.text: Claude explicitly rejects the variable annuity as a bad deal and says so directly, not just 'here are some concerns to consider'
expectations.evidence: No. Don't do this rollover. This is one of the most commonly flagged bad deals in personal finance

expectations.text: Claude explains that tax-deferred growth inside a rollover IRA is redundant — the money is already tax-deferred, so this pitch element is misleading
expectations.evidence: Your 401(k) is already tax-deferred. Rolling it into a variable annuity does not add any new tax benefit — you already have one.

expectations.text: Claude quantifies or characterizes the total fee burden: M&E fees, subaccount expenses, and optional rider fees typically total 2-3%/year, which compounds into massive long-term drag
expectations.evidence: Total all-in annual costs in a typical broker-sold variable annuity: 2–4% per year... the difference between 3% annual fees and 0.10% fees is roughly $11,600 per year in costs

expectations.text: Claude identifies the 7-year surrender period as a serious liquidity risk — locking up $400k of retirement assets in a product you cannot exit without penalty
expectations.evidence: A 7-year surrender period on $400,000 — your entire rollover balance, presumably a significant portion of your retirement assets — is a serious constraint on your financial flexibility

expectations.text: Claude names or implies the broker's commission incentive as a reason to be skeptical of this recommendation
expectations.evidence: Variable annuities carry commission rates of 5–8% of the purchase amount... On a $400,000 rollover, that's $16,000–$32,000 in commission to your broker... That is a real conflict of interest, not a hypothetical one.
